title: Completed factors of a finite separable rank-one valued extension
statement:
Let $F$ be a field with a nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute value $|\cdot|:F\to\mathbf R_{\geq0}$ (that is, $|a|=0$ exactly for $a=0$, $|ab|=|a||b|$, $|a+b|\leq\max(|a|,|b|)$, and some $a$ has $|a|\notin\{0,1\}$) [def-weil-field], let $A=\{a\in F:|a|\leq1\}$ be its valuation ring [def-trf-valuation-ring], and let $E/F$ be finite separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. Put $C=\{x\in E:x\text{ satisfies a monic polynomial in }A[T]\}$, the integral closure [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. There are finitely many distinct maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_r$ of $C$, with $r\geq1$, and these are all its maximal ideals. The rings $C_{\mathfrak m_i}$ are exactly the valuation rings of $E$ extending $A$, and their residue fields are $C/\mathfrak m_i$. Each is induced by a unique absolute value $|\cdot|_i$ extending that of $F$; write $E_i$ for this valued field and $\widehat E_i$ for its metric completion (the field of equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences, with the extended absolute value, in which $E_i$ is dense). For the metric completion $\widehat F$ of $F$, the canonical map
$$E\otimes_F\widehat F\longrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^r\widehat E_i,\qquad x\otimes a\longmapsto(xa)_i$$
is an isomorphism of $\widehat F$-algebras. The valuation ring $\widehat A$ of $\widehat F$ is henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. In every finite extension of $\widehat F$ its integral closure is the unique valuation ring extending $\widehat A$. In $\widehat E_i$ it is the ring of elements of absolute value at most one. If $x\in C$ generates $E$ over $F$, then its monic minimal polynomial $f$ belongs to $A[T]$ and factors in $\widehat F[T]$ as $f=\prod_i f_i$, where $f_i\in\widehat A[T]$ is the monic minimal polynomial of the image $x_i\in\widehat E_i$, of degree $[\widehat E_i:\widehat F]$. Every root of $f_i$ in an algebraic closure endowed with the extending absolute value has absolute value $|x|_i$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, proof, printed pp. 11--12: semilocal normalization, completed tensor-product decomposition, factors f_i and henselianity of the complete field. Primary text https://arxiv.org/html/0707.3953v3#S2.SS2.

proof.text: First normalize any valuation ring $W$ in an algebraic extension $H/F$ with $W\cap F=A$. Order $\Gamma=H^\times/W^\times$ multiplicatively, so $[z]\leq1$ means $z\in W$. The subgroup $F^\times/A^\times$ identifies with $|F^\times|$. By [lem-trf-valuation-value-group-torsion], every $\gamma=[z]$ has $\gamma^n=[a]$ for some $n>0$ and $a\in F^\times$. Define $w(z)=|a|^{1/n}$ and $w(0)=0$. This is independent of choices: if also $\gamma^m=[b]$, then $a^m/b^n\in W^\times\cap F=A^\times$, so $|a|^m=|b|^n$. Taking common powers proves multiplicativity and order preservation, strictly so because $|a|=1$ forces $\gamma^n=1$ and an ordered group is torsion-free. The valuation-ring inequality for classes follows directly from $z/t\in W\Rightarrow(z+t)/t\in W$; thus $w(z+t)\leq\max(w(z),w(t))$. Its unit ball is exactly $W$ and it extends $|\cdot|$. Any other extending absolute value with unit ball $W$ is $1$ on $W^\times$ and must satisfy $w(z)^n=|a|$, proving uniqueness. This argument needs algebraicity, not separability.

source.place: §2.1, valuation equivalence and finite algebraic extensions; explicit normalization argument

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-valuation-normalization-localizations] to $A\subset F\subset E$. It gives that $C$ is a nonzero domain with fraction field $E$, a nonempty set of maximal ideals, and the bijection $\mathfrak m\mapsto C_{\mathfrak m}$ onto extending valuation rings. Step 1 makes these equivalently the extending real absolute values. For a maximal $\mathfrak m$, reduction gives $C_{\mathfrak m}/\mathfrak mC_{\mathfrak m}\cong C/\mathfrak m$: an element $s\notin\mathfrak m$ already has invertible residue in the field $C/\mathfrak m$, so $c/s$ maps to $\bar c/\bar s$. We prove finiteness of this set below, without assuming that $C$ is finite over $A$.

source.place: §2.1, paragraph preceding Lemma 2.1.2; Proposition 2.2.1, converse, first paragraph

proof.text: Put $K=\widehat F$ and $N=E\otimes_F K$. By [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension], $N$ has dimension $d=[E:F]\geq1$ over $K$; by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-separable-tensor-field-reduced] it is reduced. It is Noetherian: an ascending chain of ideals is a chain of subspaces, whose dimensions increase at every strict inclusion and are bounded by $d$. Multiplication by a nonzerodivisor is an injective endomorphism of this finite-dimensional space, hence surjective, so the nonzerodivisor is a unit. Therefore $Q(N)=N$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-noetherian-total-ring-fractions] to obtain a $K$-algebra decomposition $N\cong\prod_{j=1}^t L_j$ with $t\geq1$ and every $L_j/K$ finite. The maps preserve $K$ because the cited decomposition is compatible with the maps from $N$. Every map $E\to L_j$, $e\mapsto\pi_j(e\otimes1)$, is a unital field map, hence injective.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, completed separable algebra; algebraic construction of its field factors

proof.text: Give each $L_j$ the extending nonarchimedean absolute value of [lem-trf-spectral-norm-algebraic-extension]. It is complete by [lem-per-finite-normed-space-complete], since $K$ is complete, its norm is nontrivial on $F$, and $L_j/K$ is finite. Use [lem-zl-finite-separable-tensor-primitive-presentation] with $k=F$, $K=\widehat F$: there is a primitive $\alpha\in E$ such that $N=K[\alpha\otimes1]$ (interchange tensor factors in the displayed presentation). Consequently $L_j=K[\alpha_j]$. If $y=\sum_{h=0}^n b_h\alpha_j^h$, choose $a_{h,m}\in F$ converging to each $b_h\in K$. Then $\sum_h a_{h,m}\alpha_j^h$ lies in the image of $E$ and its distance to $y$ is at most $\max_h|a_{h,m}-b_h|\,|\alpha_j|^h$, tending to zero. Thus $E$ is dense in $L_j$. The map from its metric completion sends a Cauchy class $[e_m]$ to $\lim_m e_m$ in $L_j$; definiteness of the distance gives injectivity, density gives surjectivity, and limits preserve addition and multiplication. It is therefore a $K$-algebra isomorphism from the completion for the restricted absolute value to $L_j$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, proof: identify each algebraic factor with the corresponding completion

proof.text: Conversely take any extending absolute value $v$ on $E$ and let $H$ be its metric completion. Sending a Cauchy sequence in $F$ to the same sequence in $E$ embeds $K$ isometrically into $H$. The map $q_v:N\to H$, $e\otimes b\mapsto eb$, is a unital $K$-algebra map. In the product decomposition of Step 3 its coordinate idempotents are orthogonal and sum to $1$. A field has only idempotents $0,1$, so exactly one maps to $1$. Hence $q_v$ factors through a field embedding $L_j\hookrightarrow H$. Its image is finite-dimensional over $K$ with the norm inherited from $H$, and is complete by [lem-per-finite-normed-space-complete]. It is closed: any sequence from the image converging in $H$ is Cauchy there, converges in the image by completeness, and the two limits agree. Since the image contains the dense subfield $E$, it equals $H$. The pullback of the norm of $H$ to $L_j$ agrees with its spectral norm by [lem-sfb-algebraic-absolute-value-unique], since both extend the given norm on the complete field $K$. Therefore $v$ is precisely the restriction constructed in Step 4.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, proof: all completed valuations arise from algebraic factors

proof.text: Different $j$ give different restrictions to $E$. Indeed, if two restrictions agreed, the maps of Step 4 would identify both $L_j$ and $L_k$ with the same Cauchy completion by isomorphisms fixing $E$ and $K$. The induced maps $N\to H$ would agree on every $e\otimes b$, hence have the same kernel. But a coordinate idempotent is in exactly one of the two coordinate kernels, a contradiction. Steps 4--5 give a bijection between the finite nonempty set of factors and the absolute values; Step 2 identifies this set with all maximal ideals of $C$. Enumerate it by $i=1,\ldots,r$. Combining the coordinate isomorphisms identifies $N$ with $\prod_i\widehat E_i$, and its $i$th component sends $e\otimes b$ to $eb$ because each identification fixes $E$ and $K$. This proves the specified canonical algebra isomorphism, not just an abstract isomorphism of products.

For henselianity put $R=\widehat A=\{b\in K:|b|\leq1\}$ and $\mathfrak n=\{|b|<1\}$. The valuation inequalities show that $R$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$: precisely its norm-one elements are units. Let $g\in R[T]$ be monic and $\bar a$ a simple root of its residue polynomial. Choose a lift $a_0\in R$, so $\rho=|g(a_0)|<1$ and $|g'(a_0)|=1$. If $g(a_0)=0$ we are done; otherwise set $a_{n+1}=a_n-g(a_n)/g'(a_n)$. For $a,h\in R$, binomial expansion gives $g(a+h)=g(a)+g'(a)h+h^2 B$ and $g'(a+h)-g'(a)=hD$ with $B,D\in R$. Induction therefore gives $a_n\in R$, $|g'(a_n)|=1$, $|g(a_n)|\leq\rho^{2^n}$ and $|a_{n+1}-a_n|\leq\rho^{2^n}$. The ultrametric inequality makes $(a_n)$ Cauchy, since for $m>n$ the distance is at most $\rho^{2^n}$. Its limit $a$ exists in $K$, lies in the closed unit ball, satisfies $g(a)=0$ by the polynomial continuity estimate, and $|a-a_0|\leq\rho<1$. Thus it lifts $\bar a$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselian-local-root-lifting] to conclude that $R$ is henselian in the stated idempotent-lifting sense.

source.place: §2.1 analytic fields are henselian; explicit Newton iteration and Stacks 04GG root criterion

proof.text: Let $H/K$ now be any finite extension, including inseparable ones. By [lem-trf-spectral-norm-algebraic-extension] it has a spectral absolute value $s$. Step 1, applied with base $K$, normalizes every valuation ring extending $R$. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-absolute-value-unique], every such normalized absolute value is $s$, so its ring is $W=\{z:s(z)\leq1\}$. Apply [lem-trf-valuation-normalization-localizations] to the integral closure $D$ of $R$ in $H$. Its maximal ideals are nonempty and their localizations are exactly these extending valuation rings, with unique maximal ideal for each such ring. Thus $D$ has one maximal ideal and $D=D_{\mathfrak n_D}=W$. Taking $H=\widehat E_i$ is legitimate by Steps 3--6, which proved this field is finite over $K$. Its existing absolute value equals $s$ by uniqueness; hence $D$ is its closed unit ball, as claimed.

source.place: §2.1 unique extension for henselian valued fields; Proposition 2.2.1 integral-closure assertion

proof.text: Suppose $x\in C$ and $E=F(x)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-valuation-ring-normal], $A$ is integrally closed, and $C$ has fraction field $E$ by Step 2. Applying [lem-sfb-integral-minpoly-fraction-descent] to $A\subset C$ shows that the monic minimal polynomial $f$ of $x$ belongs to $A[T]$. Let $d=\deg f$. By [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-polynomial-quotient-field-iso], $E=F[x]$ and $1,x,\ldots,x^{d-1}$ is a basis (division by the monic $f$ spans the quotient; a relation of smaller degree contradicts minimality). By [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension] its tensor images form a $K$-basis of $N$. Thus evaluation $K[T]\to N$, $T\mapsto x\otimes1$, is surjective with kernel $(f)$, and projection to $L_i=\widehat E_i$ is surjective with kernel $(f_i)$, where $f_i$ is the monic minimal polynomial of $x_i$. The same quotient-basis argument gives $\deg f_i=[L_i:K]$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, minimal polynomial and its completed factors; Stacks 00H7 normal-domain descent

proof.text: Each $f_i$ divides $f$, by division with remainder and minimality at $x_i$. A minimal polynomial is irreducible: a nontrivial factorization would give a smaller-degree vanishing factor in the field $L_i$. The ideals $(f_i)$ are distinct, because the coordinate kernels in $N$ are distinct and $K[T]\to N$ is surjective. Hence these distinct monic irreducibles are pairwise coprime; repeated Euclidean division (Bezout) gives $\prod_i f_i\mid f$. On the other hand, $\sum_i\deg f_i=\sum_i[L_i:K]=\dim_KN=d$, by the product decomposition and Step 9's basis. Since all polynomials are monic, $f=\prod_i f_i$. The image $x_i$ is integral over $R$ because the monic relation for $x\in C$ maps from $A[T]$ to $R[T]$. Its integral closure $D_i\subset L_i$ is the valuation ring from Step 8 and has fraction field $L_i$. Normality of $R$ by [lem-weil-pbc-valuation-ring-normal] and [lem-sfb-integral-minpoly-fraction-descent] applied to $R\subset D_i$ give $f_i\in R[T]$.

Fix an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $K$ with an extending absolute value, and any root $\beta\in\Omega$ of $f_i$. The polynomial-quotient isomorphism of [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-polynomial-quotient-field-iso] identifies $L_i=K(x_i)$ with $K[T]/(f_i)$. Evaluation at $\beta$ gives a field embedding $\sigma:L_i\hookrightarrow\Omega$ sending $x_i$ to $\beta$. Pulling back the given absolute value along $\sigma$ gives an absolute value on $L_i$ extending that of $K$. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-absolute-value-unique] it equals the norm already on $L_i$, so $|\beta|=|x_i|=|x|_i$. This includes $x=0$ when $E=F$; in that case the polynomial is $T$ and the equality is $0=0$.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.1, proof: absolute values of conjugate roots of f_i

proof_origin.place: Temkin §2.1 and Proposition 2.2.1, read in the primary HTML at https://arxiv.org/html/0707.3953v3#S2.SS2; full assembly and Newton argument written by NJ; the named PDF is absent locally.
